name: Salicylic acid peel

lead: A salicylic acid peel is the superficial peel most often used for acne and some pigmentation. People use it for clearer pores, fewer breakouts and fewer marks.

Salicylic acid is a beta-hydroxy acid described as antibacterial, anti-inflammatory and oil-soluble, which is why it is associated with acne-prone skin. Studies commonly use 20 to 30% concentrations. Published work is mostly small comparative studies and registered trials, such as a 2014 study comparing pyruvic and salicylic peels on sebum secretion in 20 people with acne.

paras: A clinician applies it in the office, and it is often repeated as a series of sessions spaced weeks apart. Mild flaking is typical, and people usually keep up sunscreen and acne skincare alongside it.
Light peels commonly cause stinging, redness, irritation and dryness. Deeper peels carry higher complication risks such as pigment change.

angle.text: People use salicylic acid peels to clear acne and reduce the marks it leaves. The oil-soluble acid works into pores, easing breakouts and inflammation so skin looks clearer. Small comparative studies cover its acne use.

lead: A salicylic acid peel is a superficial chemical peel in which a clinician applies salicylic acid, a beta-hydroxy acid (BHA), to the face or body, typically at 20 to 30 percent in the published studies [1][2][3]. People use it to look clearer: the peel is aimed at blackheads and whiteheads, active breakouts, uneven tone left by acne marks, rough texture and enlarged-looking pores, and it is usually given as a short series of sessions spaced a couple of weeks apart [4][5][6].

Salicylic acid is oil-soluble and loosens the bonds between dead cells in the outer skin layer, which is why it is associated with oily, congested skin. Wikipedia describes the chemical peel category as using exfoliating acids to remove the outer layers of skin, with light peels commonly causing stinging, redness, irritation and dryness [7]. Published work on salicylic acid peels consists of small randomized and split-face trials, single-arm studies and a number of registered trials comparing it with other peels, light devices and topical creams [1][2][8][4][5][9].

Superficial peels belong to a lineage that Wikipedia traces to the Vienna dermatologist Ferdinand von Hebra in the 19th century, and a 2015 review in Clinical, Cosmetic and Investigational Dermatology describes salicylic acid as a lipid-soluble peeling agent used at 20 to 30 percent for acne, melasma, photodamage, freckles and lentigines [7][10]. A 2018 systematic review in BMJ Open pooled 12 randomized trials of chemical peels for acne and reported that commonly used peels, including salicylic acid, appeared similarly effective and well tolerated [11]. Lower-strength acid exfoliants sold for home use have spread through social media, notably a combined AHA and BHA product that went viral on TikTok [12].
infobox: Acne, comedones, melasma, post-acne scars, photodamage, ringworm [4][5][6][16][17]
Sessions every 1 to 2 weeks for several weeks to 3 months [2][5][9]
In-office procedure; lower-strength home products also exist
Glycolic, pyruvic and trichloroacetic acid peels

paras: A salicylic acid peel is classed as a superficial or light chemical peel. The solution, often in an alcohol base at 20 to 30 percent in dermatology studies, is applied to the skin for a short time and then neutralized or allowed to dry into a frosted film, after which the outer layer flakes over the following days [5][7]. Some studies use a modified form: one trial examined a 30 percent supramolecular salicylic acid preparation, and another compared a lipohydroxy acid, a lipophilic derivative of salicylic acid, with standard salicylic acid [9][6].

Salicylic acid itself has a long history. Willow bark was used for pain and fever for centuries and was also recorded in classical texts for calluses and corns; salicin was isolated from willow bark in 1828 and salicylic acid from meadowsweet in 1839, and the acid became the chemical precursor to aspirin [13]. In skin care it is used for acne, warts, psoriasis, dandruff, calluses and keratosis pilaris, and the EU limits it in cosmetic products to 2 percent in most leave-on products [13].

Wikipedia notes that on the skin salicylic acid makes epidermal cells shed more readily, which keeps pores from clogging and allows new cell growth [13]. Because the molecule dissolves in oil, dermatologists and product makers describe it as able to work within sebum-filled pores, a property often contrasted with water-soluble alpha-hydroxy acids such as glycolic acid [7]. One study measured the skin surface lipid film directly and compared the effect of 30 percent salicylic and 50 percent pyruvic peels on sebum secretion [1].

Wikipedia credits Ferdinand von Hebra (1816 to 1880), founder of the Vienna School of Dermatology, with introducing chemical resurfacing in the second half of the 19th century, using agents such as phenol and nitric acid. It reports that phenol-croton oil peels were reportedly used discreetly by early Hollywood stars in the 1920s and were brought into mainstream practice by Thomas Baker and Howard Gordon in the 1960s [7].

Salicylic acid itself was isolated from meadowsweet in 1839, after salicin was isolated from willow bark in 1828 [13]. In the peeling literature, Kligman and Kligman used salicylic acid as a superficial peel in 50 women with mild to moderate photodamage and reported smoother surfaces, improved pigmentation and fewer fine lines, and Grimes later reported on 20% and 30% peels in patients with acne, melasma or post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, including darker skin types [10]. BHA peels became more popular as an alternative to stronger AHA peels, a trend Wikipedia attributes to salicylic acid's oil solubility, though that statement is tagged as needing a citation there [7].

sections.h: Procedure as described in the literature
paras: The 2015 review describes salicylic acid as a phenolic aromatic acid that acts mainly by loosening the desmosomal junctions between epidermal cells, with comedolytic, sebum-reducing, anti-inflammatory, antimicrobial and mild anesthetic properties. It lists concentrations of 0.5 to 10 percent for acne products, 3 to 6 percent for hyperkeratotic conditions, and 20 to 30 percent in ethanol for superficial facial peels [10].

In that review, a clinician cleanses the skin, applies a few coats, and leaves the solution on for a few minutes while stinging is eased with cooling; a white frost forms that reflects precipitated salicylic acid rather than protein coagulation, and the face is then rinsed. Sessions are described as repeated every two to four weeks, with best results after about three to six sessions [10]. Preparation in the review includes assessing Fitzpatrick skin type, documenting with photographs, using sun protection, and for some patients priming with retinoids or hydroquinone [10].

Acne is the most common reason for a salicylic acid peel in the literature. In a split-face trial of 20 people with comedonal acne, a lipohydroxy acid peel and a salicylic acid peel each reduced non-inflammatory lesions over six peels at two-week intervals, by 55.6 percent and 48.5 percent respectively, with no significant difference between them [9]. A 2023 study gave 28 people with moderate-to-severe acne a 30 percent supramolecular salicylic acid peel every two weeks for two months and examined skin microbiota and inflammation alongside acne grading [6].

A 2006 study of 24 Asian adults with acne used 30 percent salicylic acid in ethanol every two weeks for three months and measured colour with a reflectance spectrophotometer; redness readings (a* value) fell significantly from the second peel onward, and lightness rose over the course, leading the authors to describe a whitening effect [5]. Registered trials have also tested salicylic acid for melasma, alone against glycolic acid and combined with 4 percent hydroquinone, and for post-acne scars against 35 percent glycolic acid [14][3][15].

In a split-face trial of 20 women, a 30 percent salicylic acid peel was followed by overnight tretinoin 0.25 percent on one side and retinol 0.25 percent on the other, repeated at week 2. Investigators rated both regimens as improving texture, roughness, pores, dryness, erythema and overall appearance at week 4 compared with baseline [4].

The main synthesis is a 2018 BMJ Open systematic review by Chen and colleagues covering 12 randomized controlled trials with 387 participants of chemical peels for acne; a meta-analysis was not possible because of heterogeneity. In its salicylic acid comparisons, trichloroacetic acid and salicylic acid showed no significant difference in total improvement; salicylic acid and phototherapy gave similar reductions in comedones and papules, with salicylic acid less effective for pustules; in one trial salicylic acid reduced comedones more than Jessner's solution; a combination of salicylic and mandelic acid was superior to glycolic acid in total acne score; and salicylic acid and pyruvic acid were similar. The authors concluded commonly used peels appear similarly effective and well tolerated, and noted limitations: very low to moderate methodological quality, small samples, varied regimens, mostly Fitzpatrick skin types I to IV, and acne scarring not evaluated [11].
A 2014 comparison of 50 percent pyruvic and 30 percent salicylic acid peels in 20 men and women aged 13 to 30 with acne measured facial sebum secretion before and after treatment [1].

A 2024 split-face trial of 30 patients with mild to moderate acne compared 30 percent salicylic acid peels every two weeks for three months with 1.4 percent silymarin cream twice daily on the other half of the face; the Global Acne Grading System score fell on both sides, with no significant difference between treatments [2]. A randomized trial in teenagers compared 10 percent salicylic acid peels with blue LED and red laser phototherapy over ten weekly sessions; both reduced comedones, papules and pustules, and phototherapy showed a larger reduction in pustules [8].

A pilot photodynamic therapy study in 18 patients with moderate to severe acne included a group that received salicylic acid peels before aminolevulinic acid treatment; the average acne grade improved by 1.75 points on a 0 to 4 scale across the study, with adverse effects limited to redness, peeling and one episode of impetiginization [16]. A small open study of 25 people with dermatophytosis (ringworm) applied 30 percent salicylic acid weekly for four weeks, and 22 of them (88 percent) showed improvement in the reported results [17].

Registered trials have compared 30 percent salicylic acid with 25 percent trichloroacetic acid in mild to moderate acne (60 participants, completed) [18], combined it with 4 percent hydroquinone for melasma in Hispanic women [14], compared it with glycolic acid for melasma [3] and for post-acne scars [15], and compared several peel types in acne [19]. Results for these registrations are not summarized in the registry records.

Earlier evidence summarized in the 2015 review consists largely of small case series: Lee and Kim treated 35 Korean patients with acne and reported prolonged erythema beyond two days in 8.8 percent and dryness in 32.3 percent, and Grimes treated 25 patients with acne, melasma or post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation with good efficacy and minimal side effects [10].

Wikipedia notes that complications rise with peel depth and can include prolonged redness, pigment changes, milia and skin thinning, and that light peels commonly cause stinging, redness, irritation and dryness [7]. In the studies above, reported effects were mostly temporary: erythema and peeling for up to five days in the photodynamic pilot, and generally good tolerance in the lipohydroxy acid comparison [9][16]. The 2006 colourimetry study recorded an initial drop in skin lightness after the first peel before the later rise [5].

Salicylates can be absorbed through the skin. Wikipedia reports that toxicity is mostly from oral overdose, that cosmetic use is described there as not posing a significant risk, and that a documented case of toxicity followed application of a 40 percent ointment over 41 percent of the body surface. It also notes the EU classifies salicylic acid as toxic to reproduction (category 2), which restricts use in children under three [13].

The 2018 systematic review reported that peels were generally well tolerated, with burning or stinging, erythema, scaling, oedema and dryness the common effects; hyperpigmentation was rare and was reported with trichloroacetic acid, salicylic acid and Jessner's solution, and acne flare-ups were reported with the salicylic and mandelic combination and with glycolic acid alone [11].

The 2015 review reports that side effects are usually mild and transient, including prolonged erythema, dryness, intense exfoliation and crusting (Grimes reported intense exfoliation in 17.6 percent and crusting in 11.7 percent, resolving in 7 to 10 days without scarring), that salicylic acid is a weak sensitizer, and that systemic salicylism, with nausea, dizziness and tinnitus, is rare and has been reported with very large treated areas and high-strength pastes. It cites work concluding that a 30 percent facial peel poses no significant systemic risk. The review classed salicylic acid as FDA pregnancy category C and advised against salicylic acid peels in pregnancy, listing alpha-hydroxy acid peels as the alternative [10]. In 20 African American and 5 Hispanic patients, about 16 percent had mild effects that resolved within 7 to 14 days [10].

Wikipedia's salicylic acid article reports a 2018 kinetic safety assessment concluding cosmetic use poses no significant systemic risk, and gives EU limits of 2 percent for most non-preservative leave-on cosmetics (0.5 percent for some leave-on and eye or lip products), with a bar on use in products for children under three other than shampoos [13].

Salicylic acid is one of the best-known acne ingredients in over-the-counter cleansers, toners and spot treatments, and forum users discuss it alongside benzoyl peroxide and retinoids. On T Nation, one poster describes the keratolytic effect of salicylic acid washes as therapeutic, with expected drying and peeling of the skin, while another asks whether others have tried BHA products [20][21]. Users with acne on the back, chest and shoulders, a pattern discussed in another thread, also frequently raise body washes and peels [22].

Viral skincare content has popularized acid exfoliation at home. Yahoo Life reported in April 2020 that a TikTok video of before-and-after acne photos reached 4.3 million views and that more than 100,000 people bought The Ordinary's AHA 30% + BHA 2% Peeling Solution in the following month; the article advises patch testing, sunscreen and use once or twice a week because the high acid content can irritate [12]. DermFND's product page states that the formula combines glycolic, lactic, tartaric, citric and salicylic acids, says the brand describes it as only for experienced acid users, and warns of burns when misused, particularly on sensitive skin [23]. Strong in-office peels and low-strength home products differ in concentration, and Wikipedia notes that both professional peels and low-strength home kits can cause skin injury [7].

lore.intro: Salicylic acid peels appear in acne and skin-texture discussions as a step up from daily BHA products, often paired with retinoids [4][20].

claims.claim: BHA gets into oily pores better than AHAs, so it suits acne and blackheads.
A peel series can fade post-acne marks and even out tone.
Peels work better when followed by a retinoid.
Salicylic peels are as good as other acne peels.
Salicylic peels are safe across skin tones.
Viral at-home acid peels can replace professional peels.
Salicylic acid absorbs enough from a peel to cause aspirin-like toxicity.

timeline.event: Ferdinand von Hebra introduces chemical resurfacing in Vienna [7].
Salicin is isolated from willow bark by Johann Andreas Buchner [13].
Salicylic acid is isolated from meadowsweet [13].
A pilot study combines salicylic acid peels with photodynamic therapy for acne [16].
A colourimetry study in Asian patients with acne reports changes in skin tone after 30% salicylic acid peels [5].
Pyruvic and salicylic peels are compared on facial sebum secretion [1].
A split-face trial studies 30% salicylic peels followed by tretinoin or retinol [4].
Supramolecular salicylic acid peel is studied for effects on skin microbiota and inflammation [6].
A comprehensive review describes salicylic acid as a superficial peeling agent at 20 to 30% [10].
BMJ Open systematic review of 12 randomized trials of chemical peels for acne is published [11].
A TikTok video drives viral interest in a home AHA and BHA peeling solution [12].
